# Key Concepts and Variables Associated with Social Anxiety

## Core Constructs and Diagnostic Criteria
Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is defined by a marked and persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or possible scrutiny by others, with fear or anxiety about such situations occurring out of proportion to the actual provocation and leading to avoidance or enduring distress or impairment in functioning.<cite id="c107227c-0">Social anxiety disorder is characterized by a marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations involving exposure to unfamiliar people or scrutiny, with attention to issues like generalized specifier, overlap with avoidant personality disorder, and developmental links (e.g., selective mutism, test anxiety)</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">DSM-IV social phobia criteria refer essentially to the disorder’s defining features of fear in and avoidance of social situations; situational indicators used in taxometric work closely correspond to these key features, including fear of unfamiliar people or possible scrutiny</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">People with SAD have severe underlying assumptions, perfectionism, increased negative thoughts, fear of evaluation by others, and low self-efficacy, which contribute to social anxiety</cite>. Social anxiety commonly involves anticipation of embarrassment or humiliation in socially evaluative contexts and can be chronic with substantial prevalence in community samples.<cite id="128944de-0">SAD is characterized by extreme and disproportionate fear or anxiety of social situations where scrutiny or evaluation may occur, often followed by persistent behavioral avoidance that impairs adaptation; lifetime prevalence ranges from 4 to 13%</cite>

## Cognitive-Affective Mechanisms
Cognitive models converge on biased information processing as central to onset and maintenance. Interpretation bias leads to viewing ambiguous social cues as negative and catastrophizing mild negative events, while attentional bias involves prioritizing social threat cues (e.g., others’ critical gaze).<cite id="128944de-0">Cognitive models emphasize information-processing biases; interpretation bias toward negative/catastrophic social meanings has meta-analytic support, and attentional bias toward social threat cues is also supported by reviews</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Models posit that dysfunctional social beliefs activate distorted negative thoughts such as fear of negative evaluation, producing excessive anxiety or avoidance; evidence supports links between social anxiety and dysfunctional beliefs, FNE, and negative self-evaluation during performance</cite> Cognitive-affective variables include:
- Fear of negative evaluation (FNE) as a dominant concern in social-evaluative contexts and a robust correlate of social anxiety.<cite id="128944de-1">Fear of negative evaluation is strongly implicated in social anxiety; social anxiety is associated with FNE and negative cognitive self-evaluation during social performance</cite>
- Negative self-schemas and cognitive distortions (e.g., beliefs about being judged as incompetent or inadequate) that prime catastrophic appraisals and heighten anxiety in anticipation or during social tasks.<cite id="128944de-4">Cognitive models emphasize beliefs about inherent critical evaluation standards and negative self-imagery; socially anxious individuals take a negative view of ambiguous situations and self-evaluation of skills, with CBT targeting these misperceptions</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Metacognitive therapy conceptualizes attentional bias and perseverative thoughts (CAS) as strategic processes shaped by metacognitive beliefs (e.g., “worry helps” or “worry is dangerous”)</cite>
- Mental imagery: vivid, negative self-focused imagery in social scenarios amplifies anxiety; preference for object/visual imagery may increase anxiety via elaborative visualization of potential mishaps.<cite id="128944de-2">When listening to negative social dialogs, visually negative self-generated images elicit more anxiety than verbal processing; high object imagery may increase anxiety by promoting visual rehearsal of feared social scenarios</cite>
- Self-focused attention (SFA) and other-focused attention (OFA): excessive internal monitoring of thoughts/bodily sensations plus monitoring of external evaluative threats constitutes attentional bias in SAD and is often automatic or strategy-driven depending on theoretical framing.<cite id="128944de-3">Self-focused attention to negative thoughts/imagery/bodily sensations and other-focused attention to environmental threats are central; attentional bias is often measured via tasks and conceptualized as automatic in some models, or as strategic processing in metacognitive accounts</cite>

## Behavioral and Physiological Variables
Avoidance and escape/curtailing behaviors are central: anticipating scrutiny leads to avoidance of feared social situations or performance contexts, which temporarily reduces anxiety but maintains fear and impairs functioning over time (e.g., at work, school, or in relationships).<cite id="128944de-0">Social anxiety is usually followed by persistent behavioral avoidance that perpetuates fear and impairs adaptation in life domains</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Low self-efficacy and perfectionism contribute to avoidance and safety behaviors that can reinforce social anxiety and hinder effective processing of emotional information</cite> Physiological arousal (tachycardia, diaphoresis, dyspnea) often accompanies anxiety responses in social-evaluative contexts and is a target of cognitive-behavioral interventions to disrupt avoidance cycles.<cite id="c107227c-4">Structural modeling integrates cognitive, metacognitive, and behavioral aspects (including physiological arousal-related processes), with findings consistent with models positing fear of negative evaluation, low efficacy, and avoidance</cite> Functional impairment variables include reduced social participation, occupational or academic avoidance, and diminished quality of life when avoidance and distress are chronic.<cite id="128944de-0">Avoidance impeding adaptation across social settings is a hallmark, with SAD considered highly chronic and common with prevalence 4–13%</cite>

## Dimensions and Measures
Validated measures operationalize core variables and subdimensions:
- Social Anxiety Scale (SAS/SAS-A): self-report instruments covering general and performance-specific social anxiety, with subscales for FNE, avoidance/distress in new social situations, and general social avoidance; widely used across children/adolescents and adults with acceptable reliability and validity.<cite id="7d943d70-0">The SAS assesses social anxiety in domains of social, intellectual, physical, and appearance skills with high internal consistency (α≈0.90) and satisfactory validity; a subset (social and physical skills) can be used to focus on interaction vs. non-interaction contexts</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-2">SAS-A (22 items) yields total and subscale scores (18 items on anxiety plus 4 fillers), with subscales indexing FNE, avoidance/distress in new social situations, and generalized avoidance/distress</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-4">Shortened SAS-A (12 items) yields subscales for FNE, new social situations, and general social avoidance, with total range 12–60 and Cronbach’s α≈0.93 in a study sample</cite>
- Social Phobia Scale (SPS) and Social Anxiety Scale for Children/Parents (SCAS/SCAS-P): brief measures emphasizing fear of scrutiny, public speaking, and peer interactions; commonly used to index social interaction anxiety and performance situation anxiety in youth, with acceptable internal consistency across informants.<cite id="7d943d70-3">SCAS-C/P assesses anxiety across domains via child and parent reports; a 6-item social scale used in a study showed acceptable reliability, with higher scores indicating higher social anxiety</cite>
Key measurement variables capture:
- Severity and functional impact (total anxiety scores).
- FNE (anticipation of being judged poorly).
- Context specificity (interactional vs performance situations).
- Avoidance/distress in new or unfamiliar social settings (novelty sensitivity).
- Safety behaviors (reported protective actions) as related but distinct from anxiety, often measured via subscales or inventories and modeled as maintaining variables.<cite id="128944de-1">Cognitive models predict that safety behaviors and avoidance are maladaptive coping strategies that maintain social anxiety alongside dysfunctional beliefs and FNE</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Immune/protective behaviors (safety behaviors) can produce negative social reactions and impede effective processing; cognition directly and significantly impacts social anxiety</cite>

## Etiology and Development
Integrative models link early temperament and environmental factors to later anxiety and maintenance. Risk factors include shyness/withdrawal temperament, parental overcontrol or criticism, and peer victimization, which shape negative self-beliefs and threat appraisals that generalize across social contexts.<cite id="c107227c-1">An integrated aetiological and maintenance (IAM) model unites risk factors (temperament, social learning, cognition) and maintaining factors (avoidance, cognition), with empirical support for each factor’s association with social anxiety and SAD</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Process models emphasize attention to anxiety, negative self-view as social object, overestimated negative outcomes, and underestimated control/skills, leading to avoidance and safety behaviors</cite> Developmental observations show continuity from childhood selective mutism or test anxiety to social phobia, with overlapping features that complicate categorical classification and motivate dimensional approaches.<cite id="c107227c-0">Generalized specifier and overlap with avoidant personality disorder are debated; developmental issues include links with selective mutism and test anxiety</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">Taxometric work using situational indicators suggests social phobia’s continuous nature, aligning with overlapping DSM criteria and supporting dimensional latent structure</cite>

## Moderators, Mediators, and Comorbidity
Cognitive-affective mechanisms and behavioral responses interact: dysfunctional cognitive schemes (e.g., social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, catastrophe) correlate with severity of social anxiety and co-occurring anxiety disorders, suggesting shared pathways and targets for intervention.<cite id="c107227c-3">In individuals with SAD and comorbid anxiety, dysfunctional schemas (social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, catastrophe) correlate with social anxiety severity and comorbidity; these cognitive-emotional-behavioral responses explain variability</cite> Safety behaviors and appraisals moderate outcomes: engaging in safety behaviors can reduce immediate anxiety but reinforce avoidance and negative self-schemas, whereas metacognitive strategies that reduce fusion with worry/imagery may improve symptoms.<cite id="c107227c-4">Safety behaviors and avoidance are linked to vicious cycles that hinder adaptive processing; cognition directly impacts social anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Metacognitive beliefs about worry and control (e.g., “worry is dangerous”) influence CAS processes (worry/rumination, attentional bias), offering intervention targets</cite> Comorbidity is common with other anxiety disorders (e.g., generalized anxiety, panic symptoms), and higher levels of general anxiety and distress are observed in SAD, consistent with overlapping cognitive-affective vulnerabilities.<cite id="c107227c-3">Individuals with SAD exhibit higher clinical anxiety and distress; correlations exist between dysfunctional schemas and both social anxiety and comorbid psychopathology</cite>

## Putting Variables Together: A Working Model
Across models, key variables co-occur and influence one another: negative self-schemas and FNE prime catastrophic interpretation of social cues; attentional bias and self-focused monitoring amplify arousal; avoidance and safety behaviors reinforce negative appraisals; and comorbid cognitive-emotional schemes deepen dysfunction. Measurement captures these through FNE, avoidance, novelty sensitivity, and physiological arousal proxies, while developmental risk factors (temperament and caregiving/peer contexts) seed enduring patterns. Interventions aim to reduce fusion with anxious thoughts (metacognitive strategies), retrain attentional biases, challenge dysfunctional beliefs, and gradually confront feared situations to break avoidance cycles and improve self-efficacy.<cite id="128944de-0">Information-processing biases (interpretation and attention) are key to etiology/maintenance, with avoidance perpetuating fear and impairment</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Models predict that dysfunctional beliefs, fear of negative evaluation, and maladaptive coping (avoidance/safety behaviors) maintain social anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Attentional bias and metacognitive beliefs are key targets; reducing perseveration and threat-monitoring strategies can alter CAS processes</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Integrated models show cognitive, metacognitive, and behavioral factors (including self-efficacy and avoidance) explain SAD, aligning with CBT targets</cite>

## Practical Variables for Assessment and Intervention
- Clinical constructs: fear of negative evaluation, avoidance/escape, anticipatory anxiety, functional impairment, and cognitive distortions (e.g., “I’ll embarrass myself”).<cite id="128944de-0">Situations involving scrutiny provoke intense fear, followed by avoidance that impairs functioning</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Dysfunctional social beliefs and FNE are central drivers of anxiety and avoidance</cite>
- Cognitive variables: interpretation bias (ambiguity → negative/catastrophic), self-focused attention, other-focused attention, negative self-schemas, metacognitive beliefs about worry/imagery, and mental imagery vividness/catastrophizing.<cite id="128944de-0">Interpretation and attentional biases have supportive evidence (meta-analytic/large effect sizes)</cite> <cite id="128944de-2">Vivid negative self-imagery and object imagery preferences can heighten anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">SFA/OFA and metacognitive control of CAS processes are key targets</cite>
- Behavioral variables: avoidance and safety behaviors, performance avoidance, and social withdrawal; physiological arousal as proximal markers during exposure.<cite id="128944de-0">Avoidance impeding adaptation across life domains</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Safety behaviors can backfire and maintain anxiety; cognition–behavior link is strong</cite>
- Dimensional/measurement variables: total and subscale scores (FNE, interaction vs performance), context-specific scales (SAS/SAS-A, SCAS), and indices of self-efficacy and safety behaviors to track change and mechanism.<cite id="7d943d70-0">SAS subscales and psychometrics across domains</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-2">SAS-A subscales for FNE, new social situations, and generalized avoidance</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-3">SCAS subscale reliability</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Self-efficacy and avoidance embedded in integrated models</cite>
- Etiological variables: temperament shyness/overcontrol, parental overinvolvement/criticism, and peer victimization that shape appraisal and avoidance patterns across development.<cite id="c107227c-1">IAM model integrates temperament, parental/caregiving, peer, and cognitive factors in SAD</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">Dimensional perspective aligns with developmental continuity (e.g., selective mutism, test anxiety)</cite>

In sum, social anxiety is best understood as a multifactorial construct in which biased cognitions (especially FNE and catastrophic interpretations), attentional biases, negative self-schemas and imagery, avoidance and safety behaviors, and physiological arousal dynamically interact; developmental risk factors seed enduring patterns that are captured by multi-dimensional measures and targeted by cognitive-behavioral and metacognitive strategies.<cite id="c107227c-1">An integrated model ties etiological and maintenance factors with empirical support across the cognitive-affective-behavioral domains</cite> <cite id="128944de-0">Across models and evidence, interpretation and attentional biases, avoidance, and impairment are core</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-0">Measures like SAS operationalize these variables across social and performance domains</cite>

Title: Social anxiety disorder: questions and answers for the DSM‐V
Snippet: This review evaluates several issues pertaining to the diagnostic criteria for social phobia or social anxiety disorder (SAD) ( Table 1), in light of empirical evidence gathered since DSM-IV. The review was guided by questions posed in the DSM-IV Sourcebook (Vol. 2), chapters titled ''Social phobia'' [1] and ''Social phobia subtypes,'' [2] a review conducted as part of the DSM-V Stress Induced and Fear Circuitry Disorders Workgroup Conference, titled ''Social Phobia: Towards DSM V,'' [3] by questions posed by the DSM-V Anxiety, OC Spectrum, Posttraumatic, and Dissociative Disorder Work Group and by issues raised by consulted experts and advisors. The main issues to be addressed are the generalized specifier and its alternatives, the overlap with avoidant personality disorder, and developmental issues including the relationship that SAD shows in childhood with selective mutism (SM) and test anxiety.
</snippet>

Title: The aetiology and maintenance of social anxiety disorder: A synthesis of complimentary theoretical models and formulation of a new integrated model.
Snippet: BACKGROUND
Within maintenance models of social anxiety disorder (SAD), a number of cognitive and behavioural factors that drive the persistence of SAD have been proposed. However, these maintenance models do not address how SAD develops, or the origins of the proposed maintaining factors. There are also models of the development of SAD that have been proposed independently from maintenance models. These models highlight multiple factors that contribute risk to the onset of SAD, but do not address how these aetiological factors may lead to the development of the maintaining factors associated with SAD.


METHODS
A systematic review of the literature was conducted to identify aetiological and maintenance models of SAD. We then united key factors identified in these models and formulated an integrated aetiological and maintenance (IAM) model of SAD. A systematic review of the literature was then conducted on the components of the IAM model.


RESULTS
A number of aetiological and maintaining factors were identified in models of SAD. These factors could be drawn together into the IAM model. On balance, there is empirical evidence for the association of each of the factors in the IAM model with social anxiety or SAD, providing preliminary support for the model.


LIMITATIONS
There are relationships between components of the IAM model that require empirical attention. Future research will need to continue to test the IAM model.


CONCLUSIONS
The IAM model provides a framework for future investigations into the development and persistence of SAD.
</snippet>

Title: A taxometric investigation of the latent structure of social anxiety disorder in outpatients with anxiety and mood disorders
Snippet: Whereas the qualities we have described enhance the validity and value of this study, the generalizability of its results is limited by the predominately Caucasian composition of the sample. Given findings that social anxiety takes alternative symptomatic forms crossculturally [Klienknecht et al., 1997;McNeil et al., 1999], further research is needed to replicate the results of this study in other populations. Additionally, it should be noted that DSM-IV criteria for social phobia were not utilized to construct indicator sets in this study because, unlike the criteria of other diagnoses (e.g., major depressive disorder, GAD), social phobia diagnostic criteria are highly overlapping and refer essentially to the disorder's defining features of fear in and avoidance of social situations. Because this high overlap and unidimensionality make the criteria unsuitable for the construction of multiple indicators that would be appropriate for taxometric analysis (e.g., excessively high nuisance covariance), situational indicators were instead used to facilitate taxometric feasibility. Nevertheless, the indicators of social situational fear correspond closely to the key features of DSM-IV social anxiety disorder (e.g., ''marked and persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or to possible scrutiny by others''). 

Further corroboration of the dimensional latent structure of social phobia would have important implications for how the disorder is conceptualized, classified, and treated. Empirical evidence of social phobia's continuous nature may provide insight into its etiology and maintenance, thereby facilitating the development of effective assessments and treatments, and the development of a more robust understanding of other expressions of negative affect in the context of social situations.
</snippet>

Title: Pathogenetic mechanisms of comorbid anxiety disorders in persons with social anxiety disorder: the role of dysfunction cognitive schemes
Snippet: Background. Anxiety disorders are one of the common categories of mental health problems characterized by a persistent debilitating feeling of anxiety, which is due mainly to unproductive expectations about potential challenges or threats. For example, for people with social anxiety disorder, the fear of social situations can feel so intense that it seems out of their control, leading to a tendency toward social isolation and complicating the recovery process. Methods. An empirical study was conducted between 2018 and 2022 among individuals (aged 18-40) with social anxiety disorder and with clinically significant symptoms of co-occurring anxiety disorders (including generalized anxiety disorder and symptoms of panic attacks) according to DSM-5 criteria - the main the group consisted of 651 people. All study participants participated voluntarily and provided informed consent. Results. Individuals with social anxiety disorder exhibit higher levels of clinical anxiety and general distress compared to controls. Significant differences in the intensity of early dysfunctional schemes were also found compared to the control group. Correlations between manifestations of dysfunctional schemas, levels of social anxiety and manifestations of comorbid psychopathology have been demonstrated. It has been suggested that the contribution of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses related to schemas such as social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, and catastrophe anticipation may explain the distribution of variability in social anxiety symptoms and comorbid anxiety symptoms. Conclusions. The analysis of the results of the empirical study confirms the close relationship between dysfunctional beliefs and the severity of anxiety psychopathology in individuals with social anxiety disorder. Considering the features of the functioning of deep beliefs about oneself and social interaction, structured into cognitive schemes, can contribute to a practical approach to therapy and improve the quality of life of persons with the specified symptoms. Further research can be directed at expanding the role of early dysfunctional schemes in the pathogenesis of comorbid conditions and the role of avoidance mechanisms in adapting to life circumstances.
</snippet>

Title: MODEL OF SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER: A STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING OF COGNITIVE, META-COGNITIVE, BEHAVIORAL ASPECTS
Snippet: The aim of this study was to develop and validate cognitive, meta-cognitive, and behavioral model for explaining social anxiety disorder. To develop the model based on theoretical and research background (Neenan & Dryden, 2004;Bandura, 1997;Beck, 1976;Wells, 2009;Leahy, 2003), the model was developed and examined in terms of structural validity and reliability of the data. In this model, cognitive (self-efficacy, underlying assumptions, and fear of negative evaluation), meta-cognitive (mental control, negative meta-beliefs, cognitive abilities), and behavioral (safety behavior and behavioral avoidance) aspects are included in the explanation of social anxiety disorder, and the results showed an adequate fit model with the data. Considering that the previously conducted researches has not presented all of these variables together in one model, and neither has this study, so it is not possible to compare this model to those from other conducted researches. However, we can suggest that the findings of this study are in line with the results of studies conducted by Moree (2010), Gaudiano and Herbert (2003), Rapee and Heimberg (1997), Clark andWells (1995), andMasoudnia (2008). 

People with social anxiety disorder, have severe underlying assumptions, perfectionism, negative and irrational causes that are the natural processes of the mind are associated with cognitive distortions and errors, and increased negative thoughts, fear of evaluation by others, and low self-efficacy in them. 

On the one hand, cognitive interaction with negative beliefs in a higher level of cognitive processes for encountering new situations is associated with mental confusion. In behavior aspect, avoidance from frightening situations in anxiety disorders would end in defeat in cases that aren't dangerous. Immune and protective behaviors in these patients leads to a vicious negative social reaction, since many of these strategies (avoidance behavior and safety behavior) are non-controversial, therefore barriers to deal with horrible social situations, as a result can hinder the efficient processing of emotional information. The coefficient cognition direct impact on social anxiety disorder is significant. The findings of the study are consistent with the theory and studies of Clark and Wells (1995), Rapee and Heimberg (1997). Dysfunctional attitudes or assumptions activate the cognitive processes that have elements of vulnerability and perfectionism; therefore they cause more social anxiety.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: The Y-Worri Project: study protocol for a randomised controlled trial
Snippet: The Social Anxiety Scale for Adolescents (SAS-A) [34] will be employed in the current study to measure social anxiety symptoms. The SAS-A is a 22-item measure that consists of 18 descriptive self-statements assessing the respondent's subjective experience of social anxiety, and four filler items reflecting activity or social preferences. Each item is rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 

(not at all) to 5 (all the time). A total scale score can be obtained by summing the ratings for the 18 descriptive self-statements, with total scores ranging from 18 to 90. Title: Instant messaging communication in social anxiety: no support for the combined cognitive bias hypothesis (CCBH)
Snippet: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is characterized by extreme and disproportionate fear or anxiety of social situations where scrutiny or evaluation by others may occur (e.g., speaking in public, eating in front of others, participating in group activities), that may potentially lead to humiliation and embarrassment (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The distress and anxiety experienced by individuals with social anxiety is usually followed by persistent behavioral avoidance which only serves to perpetuate the experienced fear and anxiety, further impeding adequate adaption in various life domains and social settings (Stein & Stein, 2008). SAD is a highly chronic psychiatric condition, considered to be one of the most common anxiety disorders (Stein & Stein, 2008), with a lifetime prevalence rate ranging from 4 to 13% (Leichsenring & Leweke, 2017;Mennin et al., 2002;Stein et al., 2017). 

Cognitive models of social anxiety disorder suggest that information processing biases play a major role in the etiology and maintenance of the disorder (Clark & McManus, 2002;Clark & Wells, 1995;Heimberg et al., 2014;Heinrichs & Hofmann, 2001;Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). One bias put forward as a key factor in social anxiety is that of interpretation-the tendency to interpret ambiguous social events as negative, and to catastrophize even mildly negative social ones (Amir et al., 1998;Heimberg et al., 2014;Heinrichs & Hofmann, 2001;Stopa & Clark, 2000). Research on interpretation biases in social anxiety shows supportive evidence of a large effect size (for a review and meta-analysis see Chen et al., 2020). A second prominent cognitive bias suggested as having an important role in social anxiety is that of attention-the tendency of socially anxious individuals to allocate more attentional resources to environmental cues indicative of negative social evaluation or social threat (Clark & Wells, 1995;Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). Here, too, research finds supportive evidence (for reviews see Bantin et al., 2016;Chen & Clarke, 2017;Günther et al., 2021). 

What might be the relation between biased interpretation and attention in social anxiety?
</snippet>

Title: Incremental Validity for the Prediction of Social Anxiety by Personality Dimensions and Negative Social Cognitions: Testing a Process Model of Social Anxiety
Snippet: To date, several cognitive models of social anxiety have been proposed (Clark & Wells, 1995;Hofmann, 2007; see also Heimberg et al., 2014;Leigh & Clark, 2018;Modini & Abbott, 2016;Wong et al., 2014). According to Clark and Well's model (1995; see also Wells, 2007;Ghasemi et al., 2024;Wong et al., 2014) when a person with social anxiety enters a potentially social anxiety provoking situation, pre-existing dysfunctional social beliefs about himself/herself activate distorted negative thoughts, such as fear of negative evaluation by others. Although these are highly exaggerated, they are perceived as true and accurate by the individual. Consequently, the individual responds with excessive anxiety (recognized as social anxiety), and/ or avoidance. Relatedly, a psychological maintenance model of social anxiety was proposed by Hofmann (2007; see also Hofmann, 2025;Hofmann et al., 2014). This model argued that when in socially provoking situations, individuals prone to social anxiety tend to focus their attention on their own anxiety, view themselves negatively as a social object, overestimate the negative outcomes of their social behavior, and underestimate their capacity to control their emotional response and their social skills to deal effectively with the social situation. To avoid social mishaps, they utilize maladaptive coping strategies, such as avoidance and safety behaviors. 

There is sufficient evidence supporting cognitive models of social anxiety (Hodson et al., 2008;Morrison & Heimberg, 2013;Schultz & Heimberg, 2008). Furthermore, there are now data consistent with predictions from cognitive models showing that social anxiety is associated with dysfunctional social beliefs (Gros & Sarver, 2014;McCarthy & Morina, 2020), fear of negative evaluation (Carleton et al., 2007;Li et al., 2023;Wong & Moulds, 2011;Zhang et al., 2022), and negative cognitive selfevaluation during social performance (Glass et al., 1982;Gomez et al., 2022;Hofmann & DiBartolo, 2000;Lin & Fan, 2023;Muris et al., 2005).
</snippet>

Title: Association between Social Anxiety and Visual Mental Imagery of Neutral Scenes: The Moderating Role of Effortful Control
Snippet: "Social anxiety, " on the other hand, is related to the fear of "social" situations and interaction with other people. Considering these differences, it is possible that, in "natural" scenes, socially anxious individuals do not necessarily generate vivid mental imagery, whereas in "social" situations, they might exhibit vivid imagery. The different functions of neutral and social information in social anxiety were observed in attentional functions (Moriya and Tanno, 2010;Yoon et al., 2015). Socially anxious individuals exhibited broadened attentional scope for neutral stimuli (e.g., letters) to process peripheral stimuli, whereas they showed narrowed attention for social stimuli (e.g., faces). It is possible that mental imagery works in a manner similar to attentional functions. Because mental imagery also has a limited capacity (Keogh and Pearson, 2017), socially anxious individuals broaden their internal attention to mental images for neutral information, which might reduce the vividness of images; whereas, narrowed internal attention for social information could help visualize the information much more vividly. Further studies need to manipulate situations to measure imagery vividness in social anxiety. 

The finding indicating a preference for processing visual mental images, especially object mental imagery in social anxiety, was consistent with the hypothesis. Previous studies have shown that high object mental imagery is related to a preference for visualizing scenes when people listen to dialogs (Blajenkova et al., 2006;Kawahara and Matsuoka, 2009). Moreover, when people listen to negative dialogs, visually negative mental images of themselves elicit more anxiety in comparison with the images generated via verbal processing (Holmes and Mathews, 2005). This indicates that socially anxious individuals with object imagery might prefer to imagine situations visually, which increases their anxiety. 

Although spatial imagery is a subsystem of visual imagery, the present results showed a negative correlation between social anxiety and spatial imagery. Based on cognitive theories (Clark and Wells, 1995;Rapee and Heimberg, 1997), socially anxious individuals take the observer perspective. Therefore, it was hypothesized that social anxiety was positively correlated with spatial imagery, which is associated with perspective transformation. The present results suggested that socially anxious individuals involuntarily take the observer perspective, whereas they have difficulty in voluntarily changing their own perspective.
</snippet>

Title: Developing the “Metacognition about Focused Attention in Social Anxiety Questionnaire”
Snippet: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is characterized by a marked fear of social and performance situations in which the individual is scrutinized by others (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Cognitive-behavioral models of social anxiety have proposed that attentional bias to social threats is central to this perceptible fear (Clark and Wells, 1995;Rapee and Heimberg, 1997). Two critical attentional processes have been identified in individuals with SAD: self-focused attention (SFA), which refers to a person's attention to inner cues like negative thoughts, negative self-imagery, and bodily sensations; and otherfocused attention (OFA), or the addressing of environmental threats such as negative evaluations by others. 

These excessive attention to the internal and external threats are expressed as "attention bias" and they have been observed in social anxiety as well as other anxiety and mood disorders. Previous studies have focused on automatic attention bias used through the use of cognitive tasks such as "emotional Stroop tasks." Attention bias has been considered an involuntary and largely automatic mechanism (Williams, Watts, MacLeod, & Mathews, 1988). Automaticity indicates that "start and end are involuntary," "little or no attention resources are required for processing," and the attribute of "not processing consciously" (Wells, 2009). However, Wells and Matthews (1994) proposed metacognitive therapy (MCT) and viewed attention bias as a reflection of strategic processing. They established that "Cognitive Attentional Syndrome (CAS)" is responsible for psychological disorders. The CAS consists of perseverative thought in the form of worry/rumination, attentional strategies of threat monitoring (attention bias), and coping behaviors that fail to provide corrective learning experiences and contribute to failures of self-regulation. According to MCT, the intervention target is the metacognition and attentional function that controls the CAS. 

Metacognition plays a role in controlling, monitoring, and evaluating thought, in which the aspect of "metacognitive beliefs" is particularly important. These beliefs may be positive (e.g., worrying helps me cope) or negative (e.g., when I start worrying, I cannot stop; my worrying is dangerous for me) (Wells & Cartwright-Hatton, 2004).
</snippet>

Title: Negative Social Cognitions in Socially Anxious Youth: Distorted Reality or a Kernel of Truth?
Snippet: Since the introduction of two cognitive-behavioral models of social anxiety in the 1990s (Clark and Wells 1995;Rapee and Heimberg 1997), a proliferation of studies have focused on the cognitive aspects of social anxiety as described in these models (Schultz and Heimberg 2008). The cognitive-behavioral models describe what happens to an individual during, or in anticipation of, a socially threatening situation, in terms of cognitive, behavioral and physical processes (Clark and Wells 1995;Rapee and Heimberg 1997). Clark and Wells (1995) primarily focus on socially anxious individuals' beliefs about the danger inherent in social situations and the processes that prevent them from changing their beliefs and ultimately, reducing their social anxiety. The core feature of Rapee and Heimberg's (1997) model is the mental representation formed by the individual of his/her external appearance and behavior as seen by the audience. This mental representation is compared with the individual's perception of the audience's standard for evaluation. The extent to which the mental representation of performance does not meet the audience's perceived standards determines the likelihood of negative evaluation and experience of anxiety. 

Of key importance in the context of the studies reviewed in this article is the way in which the cognitive models describe how socially anxious persons tend to engage in distorted processing of information related to a socialevaluative situation. Because socially anxious individuals are greatly concerned about the possibility of negative evaluation from others (Clark and Wells 1995) and assume that other people are inherently critical (Rapee and Heimberg 1997), they take a negative view of social situations and the accompanying behavioral, cognitive and somatic responses within themselves. The assumption that socially anxious persons' negative view is a distortion of reality underpins the treatment approach of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) as one of the main principles of CBT is to try to alter the individual's negative perceptions of social situations. 

In the present review, the tendency toward a negative perspective of social situations is investigated in two domains. These domains are (a) interpretation of ambiguous social situations and (b) self-evaluation of social skills and nervous behaviors (see Fig. 1).

# Key Concepts and Variables Associated with Social Anxiety

## Core Constructs and Diagnostic Criteria
Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is defined by a marked and persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or possible scrutiny by others, with fear or anxiety about such situations occurring out of proportion to the actual provocation and leading to avoidance or enduring distress or impairment in functioning.<cite id="c107227c-0">Social anxiety disorder is characterized by a marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations involving exposure to unfamiliar people or scrutiny, with attention to issues like generalized specifier, overlap with avoidant personality disorder, and developmental links (e.g., selective mutism, test anxiety)</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">DSM-IV social phobia criteria refer essentially to the disorder’s defining features of fear in and avoidance of social situations; situational indicators used in taxometric work closely correspond to these key features, including fear of unfamiliar people or possible scrutiny</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">People with SAD have severe underlying assumptions, perfectionism, increased negative thoughts, fear of evaluation by others, and low self-efficacy, which contribute to social anxiety</cite>. Social anxiety commonly involves anticipation of embarrassment or humiliation in socially evaluative contexts and can be chronic with substantial prevalence in community samples.<cite id="128944de-0">SAD is characterized by extreme and disproportionate fear or anxiety of social situations where scrutiny or evaluation may occur, often followed by persistent behavioral avoidance that impairs adaptation; lifetime prevalence ranges from 4 to 13%</cite>

## Cognitive-Affective Mechanisms
Cognitive models converge on biased information processing as central to onset and maintenance. Interpretation bias leads to viewing ambiguous social cues as negative and catastrophizing mild negative events, while attentional bias involves prioritizing social threat cues (e.g., others’ critical gaze).<cite id="128944de-0">Cognitive models emphasize information-processing biases; interpretation bias toward negative/catastrophic social meanings has meta-analytic support, and attentional bias toward social threat cues is also supported by reviews</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Models posit that dysfunctional social beliefs activate distorted negative thoughts such as fear of negative evaluation, producing excessive anxiety or avoidance; evidence supports links between social anxiety and dysfunctional beliefs, FNE, and negative self-evaluation during performance</cite> Cognitive-affective variables include:
- Fear of negative evaluation (FNE) as a dominant concern in social-evaluative contexts and a robust correlate of social anxiety.<cite id="128944de-1">Fear of negative evaluation is strongly implicated in social anxiety; social anxiety is associated with FNE and negative cognitive self-evaluation during social performance</cite>
- Negative self-schemas and cognitive distortions (e.g., beliefs about being judged as incompetent or inadequate) that prime catastrophic appraisals and heighten anxiety in anticipation or during social tasks.<cite id="128944de-4">Cognitive models emphasize beliefs about inherent critical evaluation standards and negative self-imagery; socially anxious individuals take a negative view of ambiguous situations and self-evaluation of skills, with CBT targeting these misperceptions</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Metacognitive therapy conceptualizes attentional bias and perseverative thoughts (CAS) as strategic processes shaped by metacognitive beliefs (e.g., “worry helps” or “worry is dangerous”)</cite>
- Mental imagery: vivid, negative self-focused imagery in social scenarios amplifies anxiety; preference for object/visual imagery may increase anxiety via elaborative visualization of potential mishaps.<cite id="128944de-2">When listening to negative social dialogs, visually negative self-generated images elicit more anxiety than verbal processing; high object imagery may increase anxiety by promoting visual rehearsal of feared social scenarios</cite>
- Self-focused attention (SFA) and other-focused attention (OFA): excessive internal monitoring of thoughts/bodily sensations plus monitoring of external evaluative threats constitutes attentional bias in SAD and is often automatic or strategy-driven depending on theoretical framing.<cite id="128944de-3">Self-focused attention to negative thoughts/imagery/bodily sensations and other-focused attention to environmental threats are central; attentional bias is often measured via tasks and conceptualized as automatic in some models, or as strategic processing in metacognitive accounts</cite>

## Behavioral and Physiological Variables
Avoidance and escape/curtailing behaviors are central: anticipating scrutiny leads to avoidance of feared social situations or performance contexts, which temporarily reduces anxiety but maintains fear and impairs functioning over time (e.g., at work, school, or in relationships).<cite id="128944de-0">Social anxiety is usually followed by persistent behavioral avoidance that perpetuates fear and impairs adaptation in life domains</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Low self-efficacy and perfectionism contribute to avoidance and safety behaviors that can reinforce social anxiety and hinder effective processing of emotional information</cite> Physiological arousal (tachycardia, diaphoresis, dyspnea) often accompanies anxiety responses in social-evaluative contexts and is a target of cognitive-behavioral interventions to disrupt avoidance cycles.<cite id="c107227c-4">Structural modeling integrates cognitive, metacognitive, and behavioral aspects (including physiological arousal-related processes), with findings consistent with models positing fear of negative evaluation, low efficacy, and avoidance</cite> Functional impairment variables include reduced social participation, occupational or academic avoidance, and diminished quality of life when avoidance and distress are chronic.<cite id="128944de-0">Avoidance impeding adaptation across social settings is a hallmark, with SAD considered highly chronic and common with prevalence 4–13%</cite>

## Dimensions and Measures
Validated measures operationalize core variables and subdimensions:
- Social Anxiety Scale (SAS/SAS-A): self-report instruments covering general and performance-specific social anxiety, with subscales for FNE, avoidance/distress in new social situations, and general social avoidance; widely used across children/adolescents and adults with acceptable reliability and validity.<cite id="7d943d70-0">The SAS assesses social anxiety in domains of social, intellectual, physical, and appearance skills with high internal consistency (α≈0.90) and satisfactory validity; a subset (social and physical skills) can be used to focus on interaction vs. non-interaction contexts</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-2">SAS-A (22 items) yields total and subscale scores (18 items on anxiety plus 4 fillers), with subscales indexing FNE, avoidance/distress in new social situations, and generalized avoidance/distress</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-4">Shortened SAS-A (12 items) yields subscales for FNE, new social situations, and general social avoidance, with total range 12–60 and Cronbach’s α≈0.93 in a study sample</cite>
- Social Phobia Scale (SPS) and Social Anxiety Scale for Children/Parents (SCAS/SCAS-P): brief measures emphasizing fear of scrutiny, public speaking, and peer interactions; commonly used to index social interaction anxiety and performance situation anxiety in youth, with acceptable internal consistency across informants.<cite id="7d943d70-3">SCAS-C/P assesses anxiety across domains via child and parent reports; a 6-item social scale used in a study showed acceptable reliability, with higher scores indicating higher social anxiety</cite>
Key measurement variables capture:
- Severity and functional impact (total anxiety scores).
- FNE (anticipation of being judged poorly).
- Context specificity (interactional vs performance situations).
- Avoidance/distress in new or unfamiliar social settings (novelty sensitivity).
- Safety behaviors (reported protective actions) as related but distinct from anxiety, often measured via subscales or inventories and modeled as maintaining variables.<cite id="128944de-1">Cognitive models predict that safety behaviors and avoidance are maladaptive coping strategies that maintain social anxiety alongside dysfunctional beliefs and FNE</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Immune/protective behaviors (safety behaviors) can produce negative social reactions and impede effective processing; cognition directly and significantly impacts social anxiety</cite>

## Etiology and Development
Integrative models link early temperament and environmental factors to later anxiety and maintenance. Risk factors include shyness/withdrawal temperament, parental overcontrol or criticism, and peer victimization, which shape negative self-beliefs and threat appraisals that generalize across social contexts.<cite id="c107227c-1">An integrated aetiological and maintenance (IAM) model unites risk factors (temperament, social learning, cognition) and maintaining factors (avoidance, cognition), with empirical support for each factor’s association with social anxiety and SAD</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Process models emphasize attention to anxiety, negative self-view as social object, overestimated negative outcomes, and underestimated control/skills, leading to avoidance and safety behaviors</cite> Developmental observations show continuity from childhood selective mutism or test anxiety to social phobia, with overlapping features that complicate categorical classification and motivate dimensional approaches.<cite id="c107227c-0">Generalized specifier and overlap with avoidant personality disorder are debated; developmental issues include links with selective mutism and test anxiety</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">Taxometric work using situational indicators suggests social phobia’s continuous nature, aligning with overlapping DSM criteria and supporting dimensional latent structure</cite>

## Moderators, Mediators, and Comorbidity
Cognitive-affective mechanisms and behavioral responses interact: dysfunctional cognitive schemes (e.g., social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, catastrophe) correlate with severity of social anxiety and co-occurring anxiety disorders, suggesting shared pathways and targets for intervention.<cite id="c107227c-3">In individuals with SAD and comorbid anxiety, dysfunctional schemas (social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, catastrophe) correlate with social anxiety severity and comorbidity; these cognitive-emotional-behavioral responses explain variability</cite> Safety behaviors and appraisals moderate outcomes: engaging in safety behaviors can reduce immediate anxiety but reinforce avoidance and negative self-schemas, whereas metacognitive strategies that reduce fusion with worry/imagery may improve symptoms.<cite id="c107227c-4">Safety behaviors and avoidance are linked to vicious cycles that hinder adaptive processing; cognition directly impacts social anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Metacognitive beliefs about worry and control (e.g., “worry is dangerous”) influence CAS processes (worry/rumination, attentional bias), offering intervention targets</cite> Comorbidity is common with other anxiety disorders (e.g., generalized anxiety, panic symptoms), and higher levels of general anxiety and distress are observed in SAD, consistent with overlapping cognitive-affective vulnerabilities.<cite id="c107227c-3">Individuals with SAD exhibit higher clinical anxiety and distress; correlations exist between dysfunctional schemas and both social anxiety and comorbid psychopathology</cite>

## Putting Variables Together: A Working Model
Across models, key variables co-occur and influence one another: negative self-schemas and FNE prime catastrophic interpretation of social cues; attentional bias and self-focused monitoring amplify arousal; avoidance and safety behaviors reinforce negative appraisals; and comorbid cognitive-emotional schemes deepen dysfunction. Measurement captures these through FNE, avoidance, novelty sensitivity, and physiological arousal proxies, while developmental risk factors (temperament and caregiving/peer contexts) seed enduring patterns. Interventions aim to reduce fusion with anxious thoughts (metacognitive strategies), retrain attentional biases, challenge dysfunctional beliefs, and gradually confront feared situations to break avoidance cycles and improve self-efficacy.<cite id="128944de-0">Information-processing biases (interpretation and attention) are key to etiology/maintenance, with avoidance perpetuating fear and impairment</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Models predict that dysfunctional beliefs, fear of negative evaluation, and maladaptive coping (avoidance/safety behaviors) maintain social anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">Attentional bias and metacognitive beliefs are key targets; reducing perseveration and threat-monitoring strategies can alter CAS processes</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Integrated models show cognitive, metacognitive, and behavioral factors (including self-efficacy and avoidance) explain SAD, aligning with CBT targets</cite>

## Practical Variables for Assessment and Intervention
- Clinical constructs: fear of negative evaluation, avoidance/escape, anticipatory anxiety, functional impairment, and cognitive distortions (e.g., “I’ll embarrass myself”).<cite id="128944de-0">Situations involving scrutiny provoke intense fear, followed by avoidance that impairs functioning</cite> <cite id="128944de-1">Dysfunctional social beliefs and FNE are central drivers of anxiety and avoidance</cite>
- Cognitive variables: interpretation bias (ambiguity → negative/catastrophic), self-focused attention, other-focused attention, negative self-schemas, metacognitive beliefs about worry/imagery, and mental imagery vividness/catastrophizing.<cite id="128944de-0">Interpretation and attentional biases have supportive evidence (meta-analytic/large effect sizes)</cite> <cite id="128944de-2">Vivid negative self-imagery and object imagery preferences can heighten anxiety</cite> <cite id="128944de-3">SFA/OFA and metacognitive control of CAS processes are key targets</cite>
- Behavioral variables: avoidance and safety behaviors, performance avoidance, and social withdrawal; physiological arousal as proximal markers during exposure.<cite id="128944de-0">Avoidance impeding adaptation across life domains</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Safety behaviors can backfire and maintain anxiety; cognition–behavior link is strong</cite>
- Dimensional/measurement variables: total and subscale scores (FNE, interaction vs performance), context-specific scales (SAS/SAS-A, SCAS), and indices of self-efficacy and safety behaviors to track change and mechanism.<cite id="7d943d70-0">SAS subscales and psychometrics across domains</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-2">SAS-A subscales for FNE, new social situations, and generalized avoidance</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-3">SCAS subscale reliability</cite> <cite id="c107227c-4">Self-efficacy and avoidance embedded in integrated models</cite>
- Etiological variables: temperament shyness/overcontrol, parental overinvolvement/criticism, and peer victimization that shape appraisal and avoidance patterns across development.<cite id="c107227c-1">IAM model integrates temperament, parental/caregiving, peer, and cognitive factors in SAD</cite> <cite id="c107227c-2">Dimensional perspective aligns with developmental continuity (e.g., selective mutism, test anxiety)</cite>

In sum, social anxiety is best understood as a multifactorial construct in which biased cognitions (especially FNE and catastrophic interpretations), attentional biases, negative self-schemas and imagery, avoidance and safety behaviors, and physiological arousal dynamically interact; developmental risk factors seed enduring patterns that are captured by multi-dimensional measures and targeted by cognitive-behavioral and metacognitive strategies.<cite id="c107227c-1">An integrated model ties etiological and maintenance factors with empirical support across the cognitive-affective-behavioral domains</cite> <cite id="128944de-0">Across models and evidence, interpretation and attentional biases, avoidance, and impairment are core</cite> <cite id="7d943d70-0">Measures like SAS operationalize these variables across social and performance domains</cite></answer>

Title: Social anxiety disorder: questions and answers for the DSM‐V
Snippet: This review evaluates several issues pertaining to the diagnostic criteria for social phobia or social anxiety disorder (SAD) ( Table 1), in light of empirical evidence gathered since DSM-IV. The review was guided by questions posed in the DSM-IV Sourcebook (Vol. 2), chapters titled ''Social phobia'' [1] and ''Social phobia subtypes,'' [2] a review conducted as part of the DSM-V Stress Induced and Fear Circuitry Disorders Workgroup Conference, titled ''Social Phobia: Towards DSM V,'' [3] by questions posed by the DSM-V Anxiety, OC Spectrum, Posttraumatic, and Dissociative Disorder Work Group and by issues raised by consulted experts and advisors. The main issues to be addressed are the generalized specifier and its alternatives, the overlap with avoidant personality disorder, and developmental issues including the relationship that SAD shows in childhood with selective mutism (SM) and test anxiety.

Title: The aetiology and maintenance of social anxiety disorder: A synthesis of complimentary theoretical models and formulation of a new integrated model.
Snippet: BACKGROUND
Within maintenance models of social anxiety disorder (SAD), a number of cognitive and behavioural factors that drive the persistence of SAD have been proposed. However, these maintenance models do not address how SAD develops, or the origins of the proposed maintaining factors. There are also models of the development of SAD that have been proposed independently from maintenance models. These models highlight multiple factors that contribute risk to the onset of SAD, but do not address how these aetiological factors may lead to the development of the maintaining factors associated with SAD.


METHODS
A systematic review of the literature was conducted to identify aetiological and maintenance models of SAD. We then united key factors identified in these models and formulated an integrated aetiological and maintenance (IAM) model of SAD. A systematic review of the literature was then conducted on the components of the IAM model.


RESULTS
A number of aetiological and maintaining factors were identified in models of SAD. These factors could be drawn together into the IAM model. On balance, there is empirical evidence for the association of each of the factors in the IAM model with social anxiety or SAD, providing preliminary support for the model.


LIMITATIONS
There are relationships between components of the IAM model that require empirical attention. Future research will need to continue to test the IAM model.


CONCLUSIONS
The IAM model provides a framework for future investigations into the development and persistence of SAD.

Title: A taxometric investigation of the latent structure of social anxiety disorder in outpatients with anxiety and mood disorders
Snippet: Whereas the qualities we have described enhance the validity and value of this study, the generalizability of its results is limited by the predominately Caucasian composition of the sample. Given findings that social anxiety takes alternative symptomatic forms crossculturally [Klienknecht et al., 1997;McNeil et al., 1999], further research is needed to replicate the results of this study in other populations. Additionally, it should be noted that DSM-IV criteria for social phobia were not utilized to construct indicator sets in this study because, unlike the criteria of other diagnoses (e.g., major depressive disorder, GAD), social phobia diagnostic criteria are highly overlapping and refer essentially to the disorder's defining features of fear in and avoidance of social situations. Because this high overlap and unidimensionality make the criteria unsuitable for the construction of multiple indicators that would be appropriate for taxometric analysis (e.g., excessively high nuisance covariance), situational indicators were instead used to facilitate taxometric feasibility. Nevertheless, the indicators of social situational fear correspond closely to the key features of DSM-IV social anxiety disorder (e.g., ''marked and persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or to possible scrutiny by others''). 

Further corroboration of the dimensional latent structure of social phobia would have important implications for how the disorder is conceptualized, classified, and treated. Empirical evidence of social phobia's continuous nature may provide insight into its etiology and maintenance, thereby facilitating the development of effective assessments and treatments, and the development of a more robust understanding of other expressions of negative affect in the context of social situations.

Title: Pathogenetic mechanisms of comorbid anxiety disorders in persons with social anxiety disorder: the role of dysfunction cognitive schemes
Snippet: Background. Anxiety disorders are one of the common categories of mental health problems characterized by a persistent debilitating feeling of anxiety, which is due mainly to unproductive expectations about potential challenges or threats. For example, for people with social anxiety disorder, the fear of social situations can feel so intense that it seems out of their control, leading to a tendency toward social isolation and complicating the recovery process. Methods. An empirical study was conducted between 2018 and 2022 among individuals (aged 18-40) with social anxiety disorder and with clinically significant symptoms of co-occurring anxiety disorders (including generalized anxiety disorder and symptoms of panic attacks) according to DSM-5 criteria - the main the group consisted of 651 people. All study participants participated voluntarily and provided informed consent. Results. Individuals with social anxiety disorder exhibit higher levels of clinical anxiety and general distress compared to controls. Significant differences in the intensity of early dysfunctional schemes were also found compared to the control group. Correlations between manifestations of dysfunctional schemas, levels of social anxiety and manifestations of comorbid psychopathology have been demonstrated. It has been suggested that the contribution of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses related to schemas such as social isolation/alienation, incompetence/failure anticipation, and catastrophe anticipation may explain the distribution of variability in social anxiety symptoms and comorbid anxiety symptoms. Conclusions. The analysis of the results of the empirical study confirms the close relationship between dysfunctional beliefs and the severity of anxiety psychopathology in individuals with social anxiety disorder. Considering the features of the functioning of deep beliefs about oneself and social interaction, structured into cognitive schemes, can contribute to a practical approach to therapy and improve the quality of life of persons with the specified symptoms. Further research can be directed at expanding the role of early dysfunctional schemes in the pathogenesis of comorbid conditions and the role of avoidance mechanisms in adapting to life circumstances.

Title: MODEL OF SOCIAL ANXIETY DISORDER: A STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING OF COGNITIVE, META-COGNITIVE, BEHAVIORAL ASPECTS
Snippet: The aim of this study was to develop and validate cognitive, meta-cognitive, and behavioral model for explaining social anxiety disorder. To develop the model based on theoretical and research background (Neenan & Dryden, 2004;Bandura, 1997;Beck, 1976;Wells, 2009;Leahy, 2003), the model was developed and examined in terms of structural validity and reliability of the data. In this model, cognitive (self-efficacy, underlying assumptions, and fear of negative evaluation), meta-cognitive (mental control, negative meta-beliefs, cognitive abilities), and behavioral (safety behavior and behavioral avoidance) aspects are included in the explanation of social anxiety disorder, and the results showed an adequate fit model with the data. Considering that the previously conducted researches has not presented all of these variables together in one model, and neither has this study, so it is not possible to compare this model to those from other conducted researches. However, we can suggest that the findings of this study are in line with the results of studies conducted by Moree (2010), Gaudiano and Herbert (2003), Rapee and Heimberg (1997), Clark andWells (1995), andMasoudnia (2008). 

People with social anxiety disorder, have severe underlying assumptions, perfectionism, negative and irrational causes that are the natural processes of the mind are associated with cognitive distortions and errors, and increased negative thoughts, fear of evaluation by others, and low self-efficacy in them. 

On the one hand, cognitive interaction with negative beliefs in a higher level of cognitive processes for encountering new situations is associated with mental confusion. In behavior aspect, avoidance from frightening situations in anxiety disorders would end in defeat in cases that aren't dangerous. Immune and protective behaviors in these patients leads to a vicious negative social reaction, since many of these strategies (avoidance behavior and safety behavior) are non-controversial, therefore barriers to deal with horrible social situations, as a result can hinder the efficient processing of emotional information. The coefficient cognition direct impact on social anxiety disorder is significant. The findings of the study are consistent with the theory and studies of Clark and Wells (1995), Rapee and Heimberg (1997). Dysfunctional attitudes or assumptions activate the cognitive processes that have elements of vulnerability and perfectionism; therefore they cause more social anxiety.

snippet.text:
BACKGROUND
Within maintenance models of social anxiety disorder (SAD), a number of cognitive and behavioural factors that drive the persistence of SAD have been proposed. However, these maintenance models do not address how SAD develops, or the origins of the proposed maintaining factors. There are also models of the development of SAD that have been proposed independently from maintenance models. These models highlight multiple factors that contribute risk to the onset of SAD, but do not address how these aetiological factors may lead to the development of the maintaining factors associated with SAD.


METHODS
A systematic review of the literature was conducted to identify aetiological and maintenance models of SAD. We then united key factors identified in these models and formulated an integrated aetiological and maintenance (IAM) model of SAD. A systematic review of the literature was then conducted on the components of the IAM model.


RESULTS
A number of aetiological and maintaining factors were identified in models of SAD. These factors could be drawn together into the IAM model. On balance, there is empirical evidence for the association of each of the factors in the IAM model with social anxiety or SAD, providing preliminary support for the model.


LIMITATIONS
There are relationships between components of the IAM model that require empirical attention. Future research will need to continue to test the IAM model.


CONCLUSIONS
The IAM model provides a framework for future investigations into the development and persistence of SAD.

Whereas the qualities we have described enhance the validity and value of this study, the generalizability of its results is limited by the predominately Caucasian composition of the sample. Given findings that social anxiety takes alternative symptomatic forms crossculturally [Klienknecht et al., 1997;McNeil et al., 1999], further research is needed to replicate the results of this study in other populations. Additionally, it should be noted that DSM-IV criteria for social phobia were not utilized to construct indicator sets in this study because, unlike the criteria of other diagnoses (e.g., major depressive disorder, GAD), social phobia diagnostic criteria are highly overlapping and refer essentially to the disorder's defining features of fear in and avoidance of social situations. Because this high overlap and unidimensionality make the criteria unsuitable for the construction of multiple indicators that would be appropriate for taxometric analysis (e.g., excessively high nuisance covariance), situational indicators were instead used to facilitate taxometric feasibility. Nevertheless, the indicators of social situational fear correspond closely to the key features of DSM-IV social anxiety disorder (e.g., ''marked and persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or to possible scrutiny by others''). 

Further corroboration of the dimensional latent structure of social phobia would have important implications for how the disorder is conceptualized, classified, and treated. Empirical evidence of social phobia's continuous nature may provide insight into its etiology and maintenance, thereby facilitating the development of effective assessments and treatments, and the development of a more robust understanding of other expressions of negative affect in the context of social situations.

Snippet: The Social Anxiety Scale (SAS) is a Dutch questionnaire to assess social anxiety in the context of social skills, intellectual skills, physical skills, and appearance. It is designed for children aged 8 and older. The reliability of the SAS is high (internal consistency = 0.90) [39], and its validity is satisfactory [40]. The SAS consists of 36 items, which are each followed by two options: one option indicating social anxiety and the other indicating no social anxiety. For example: 'If someone in the group looks at me when I am doing something (1) I do not become nervous, (2) I become nervous'. Higher scores indicate more social anxiety. For this study, a subset of subscales was selected in order to minimize number of variables in statistical analyses: these were 'social skills' and 'physical skills', in order to be able to contrast anxiety in contexts with and without social interactions.

Title: The Y-Worri Project: study protocol for a randomised controlled trial
Snippet: The Social Anxiety Scale for Adolescents (SAS-A) [34] will be employed in the current study to measure social anxiety symptoms. The SAS-A is a 22-item measure that consists of 18 descriptive self-statements assessing the respondent's subjective experience of social anxiety, and four filler items reflecting activity or social preferences. Each item is rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 

(not at all) to 5 (all the time). A total scale score can be obtained by summing the ratings for the 18 descriptive self-statements, with total scores ranging from 18 to 90. Higher SAS-A scores are indicative of greater social anxiety symptoms. Three subscales can also be derived from the SAS-A which measure fear of negative evaluation (FNE), social avoidance and distress with new social situations or unfamiliar peers (SAD-New), and more generalised social avoidance and distress (SAD-General).

Title: The Role of Distorted Cognitions in Mediating Treatment Outcome in Children with Social Anxiety Disorder: A Preliminary Study
Snippet: The SCAS-C/P assesses anxiety symptoms by child selfreport and parent-report for the child across multiple anxiety domains. For this study, only the 6-item social scale of the SCAS was used. Items were answered on a 4-point Likertscale (0 [never] to 3 [always]). Higher scores indicate higher social anxiety levels. The SCAS-social scale has previously demonstrated acceptable psychometric properties [35,36]. 

Internal consistency in this study was acceptable (SCAS-C: pre-treatment α = 0.82, post-treatment α = 0.69, 6-month follow-up α = 0.66; SCAS-P: pre-treatment α = 0.79, posttreatment, α = 0.84, 6-month follow-up α = 0.82).

documents.snippet:
The Social Anxiety Scale for Adolescents (SAS-A) [34] will be employed in the current study to measure social anxiety symptoms. The SAS-A is a 22-item measure that consists of 18 descriptive self-statements assessing the respondent's subjective experience of social anxiety, and four filler items reflecting activity or social preferences. Each item is rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 

(not at all) to 5 (all the time). A total scale score can be obtained by summing the ratings for the 18 descriptive self-statements, with total scores ranging from 18 to 90. Higher SAS-A scores are indicative of greater social anxiety symptoms. Three subscales can also be derived from the SAS-A which measure fear of negative evaluation (FNE), social avoidance and distress with new social situations or unfamiliar peers (SAD-New), and more generalised social avoidance and distress (SAD-General).
